sources.title: AI RMF Core: Measure
authors: National Institute of Standards and Technology
sources.authority_note: NIST's official AI Risk Management Framework resource; its Measure function specifies documented test sets, metrics, and performance criteria.

sources.title: AI Risks and Trustworthiness: Valid and Reliable
authors: National Institute of Standards and Technology
sources.authority_note: Official NIST AI RMF material defining validation as objective evidence that intended requirements are fulfilled and noting that failures can have unequal harm.

sources.title: RFC 9562: Universally Unique Identifiers (UUIDs)
sources.authority_note: IETF Standards Track specification; defines UUIDs as persistent identifiers intended to be unique without central registration.

sources.title: JSON Lines documentation
sources.authority_note: Format's canonical documentation; specifies one valid JSON value per line and newline-delimited UTF-8 records.

claims.claim: An evaluation should state an observable performance or assurance criterion and document the test set and measurement details; a prompt collection alone does not define what counts as failure.
claims.source_locator: NIST AI RMF Core, Measure 2.1 and Measure 2.3
claims.support: NIST requires documented test sets and details of tools used for TEVV, and measured criteria demonstrated under relevant conditions.
claims.scope: General AI-system evaluation and risk measurement.
claims.limitations: NIST does not prescribe the course's particular regression criterion or record fields.

claims.claim: The intended use and requirements must be made explicit so that a label records the defined failure behavior rather than unrelated preferences.
claims.source_locator: NIST AI RMF, section 3.1 Valid and Reliable; validation definition
claims.support: NIST describes validation as objective evidence that requirements for a specific intended use are fulfilled and says outputs must be interpreted in context.
claims.scope: Criterion design for a specified intended use.
claims.limitations: The exclusion of style preferences is an application example, not a NIST rule.

claims.claim: Binary labels are meaningful only after the evaluator names which class represents the target behavior; this course fixes 1 as regression present and 0 as acceptable under the criterion.
claims.source_locator: NIST AI RMF, section 3.1 Valid and Reliable; Core Measure 2.3
claims.support: NIST ties measurement to documented requirements and intended use, and requires performance or assurance criteria to be measured under relevant conditions; this supports explicit label semantics.
claims.scope: This is the course's operational binary convention.
claims.limitations: The 1/0 polarity is a course decision, not a universal standard.

claims.claim: Stable unique identifiers allow records to remain identifiable across files and processing without relying on positional order; UUIDs are a standardized option when globally unique IDs are needed.
claims.source_locator: RFC 9562, Introduction and section 1; UUID uniqueness and persistence motivation
claims.support: The RFC describes UUIDs as persistent, unique identifiers usable without centralized registration and suitable for database keys.
claims.scope: Identifier design; simple local case IDs may be sufficient for this lesson.
claims.limitations: A short human-readable case_id need not be a UUID; uniqueness still must be checked in the dataset.

claims.claim: A minimal joinable evaluation record should preserve the input, candidate output, human ground-truth label, and stable case ID; deterministic checks should reject missing or duplicate identity before downstream automation.
claims.source_locator: NIST AI RMF Core Measure 2.1; RFC 9562 Introduction
claims.support: NIST calls for documented test sets and tools, while RFC 9562 supports persistent identifiers; the exact four-field schema is a course inference.
claims.scope: EP-01 artifact interface and local validation.
claims.limitations: Sources do not mandate these exact names or JSON representation.

claims.claim: JSONL persistence can represent one evaluation record per line, and a read-back comparison is a practical integrity check for the written artifact.
claims.support: The format specifies valid JSON values per line, UTF-8 encoding, and newline termination; round-trip comparison is an implementation inference.
claims.limitations: JSONL does not itself enforce schema, unique IDs, binary labels, or class balance.

evidence_gaps: No primary source mandates this lesson's exact four-field schema or the 1=regression polarity; these are explicit course interface decisions.

No source establishes a universal minimum sample size or class-balance threshold, or directly mandates checking both classes for this dataset; US-L01-04's both-class presence check is therefore a bounded course decision, not research evidence.
